### Exercise 1: Two paths, one difference {.unnumbered .exercise-title #exercise-l01-1}

::: {.exercise}
**Problem.** [core, pencil] The twelve-period economy of the notes follows
$y_t=0.5\,y_{t-1}+s_t+v_t$ with $y_0=0$, and its interventions fall at
$t=1,5,10,12$. Around the second intervention the realized path is
$y_4=0.0625$, $y_5=-0.66875$, $y_6=-0.134375$, $y_7=2.0328125$, and
$y_8=-0.28359375$, and the disturbances are $v_5=-1.7$, $v_6=0.2$, $v_7=2.1$,
and $v_8=-1.3$.

(a) Build the counterfactual path $y^{c}_t$ for $t=5,\dots,8$ by switching off
the intervention at $t=5$ and nothing else. Tabulate $y_t$, $y^{c}_t$, the gap
$y_t-y^{c}_t$, and the change since the date before, $y_t-y_4$.

(b) Split each change $y_t-y_4$ into the causal response and the change the
economy would have made without the intervention. At which dates does reading
the change as the effect get the sign wrong, and by what factor does it
overstate the effect at $t=7$?

(c) Without repeating the recursion, give the four gaps that would result if
every $v_t$ were replaced by zero, and explain why.
:::

:::: {.solution-material}
::: {.callout-tip .exercise-hint collapse="true" icon=false}
## Hint

Only one input differs between the two recursions: $s_5$ equals 1 on the
realized path and 0 on the counterfactual one. Start both paths from $y_4$,
which an intervention dated $t=5$ cannot have moved, and feed the same $v_t$
into both. For (c), subtract one recursion from the other before substituting
any number.
:::

::: {.callout-note .exercise-solution collapse="true" icon=false}
## Detailed solution

The two paths obey the same rule and receive the same disturbances:

$$
y_t=0.5\,y_{t-1}+s_t+v_t,
\qquad
y^{c}_t=0.5\,y^{c}_{t-1}+s^{c}_t+v_t,
$$

with $s^{c}_5=0$ and $s^{c}_t=s_t$ at every other date. Before $t=5$ the rule
never uses $s_5$, so the paths coincide up to that date and $y^{c}_4=y_4=0.0625$.
The plan is to run the second recursion forward from there and compare.

**(a)** Four applications of the rule give the counterfactual path:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y^{c}_5&=0.5(0.0625)+0-1.7=-1.66875,\\
y^{c}_6&=0.5(-1.66875)+0+0.2=-0.634375,\\
y^{c}_7&=0.5(-0.634375)+0+2.1=1.7828125,\\
y^{c}_8&=0.5(1.7828125)+0-1.3=-0.40859375.
\end{aligned}
$$

Every input has a short decimal expansion, so the table is exact; nothing is
rounded.

| $t$ | $y_t$ | $y^{c}_t$ | Gap $y_t-y^{c}_t$ | Change $y_t-y_4$ | $y^{c}_t-y_4$ |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 5 | −0.66875 | −1.66875 | 1 | −0.73125 | −1.73125 |
| 6 | −0.134375 | −0.634375 | 0.5 | −0.196875 | −0.696875 |
| 7 | 2.0328125 | 1.7828125 | 0.25 | 1.9703125 | 1.7203125 |
| 8 | −0.28359375 | −0.40859375 | 0.125 | −0.34609375 | −0.47109375 |

The gap is measured in units of $y$ for a one-unit intervention. Its halving
can be read off the two rules. Subtracting the counterfactual rule from the
realized one,

$$
y_t-y^{c}_t=0.5\,\bigl(y_{t-1}-y^{c}_{t-1}\bigr)+\bigl(s_t-s^{c}_t\bigr),
$$

and the disturbance has cancelled. At $t=5$ the gap is $0.5\times0+1=1$; after
that $s_t-s^{c}_t=0$, so each period keeps half of the previous gap.

**(b)** Add and subtract $y^{c}_t$:

$$
y_t-y_4=\underbrace{\bigl(y_t-y^{c}_t\bigr)}_{\text{causal response}}
+\underbrace{\bigl(y^{c}_t-y_4\bigr)}_{\text{change without the intervention}}.
$$

The last three columns of the table carry out the split. At $t=5$,
$-0.73125=1+(-1.73125)$; at $t=7$, $1.9703125=0.25+1.7203125$. The second
bracket contains no intervention at all. Iterating the counterfactual rule
from $t=4$ gives $y^{c}_7=0.5^3y_4+0.5^2v_5+0.5\,v_6+v_7=0.0078125-0.425+0.1+2.1$,
so the counterfactual change $1.7203125$ is the fading of $y_4$ plus three
disturbances, and $v_7=2.1$ alone is larger than all of it.

Reading the change as the effect gets the sign wrong at $t=5$ ($-0.73125$
against 1), at $t=6$ ($-0.196875$ against 0.5), and at $t=8$ ($-0.34609375$
against 0.125). At $t=7$ it reports $1.9703125$ against 0.25, which is
$7.88125$ times the effect. The intervention did the same thing at every date;
the disturbances did not.

**(c)** The gap recursion in (a) contains no $v_t$. Replacing every disturbance
by zero moves both paths but leaves their difference alone, so the gaps are
still 1, 0.5, 0.25, and 0.125. They are the formula $\theta_h=\theta_0\rho^h$
from the notes' section on the smallest model, with $\theta_0=1$ and $\rho=0.5$,
read at $h=0,\dots,3$. This is the check on the whole calculation: a gap that
changed when the disturbances changed would signal an arithmetic slip.

Two mistakes are common. The first is the one the lecture opens with:
reporting $y_5-y_4=-0.73125$ as the effect of the intervention. The second is to
build the counterfactual by setting $s_t=0$ at every date, as if "no
intervention" meant no interventions at all. The intervention at $t=1$ then
disappears as well, its fading contribution $0.5^{t-1}$ joins each gap, and the
gaps become 1.0625, 0.53125, 0.265625, and 0.1328125. The causal response to one
intervention removes that intervention and nothing else.
:::
::::

### Exercise 2: Iterate forward {.unnumbered .exercise-title #exercise-l01-2}

::: {.exercise}
**Problem.** [core, pencil] Let $y_t=\rho\,y_{t-1}+\theta_0s_t+v_t$, where the
interventions $s_t$ and the disturbances $v_t$ each have mean zero, are
independent over time, and are independent of each other, and $|\rho|<1$
(Assumptions A1–A4 of the notes).

(a) Substitute the rule into itself to write $y_{t+1}$ and then $y_{t+2}$ in
terms of $y_{t-1}$ and the interventions and disturbances dated $t$ onward.
State the general formula for $y_{t+h}$ and prove it by induction.

(b) Change $s_t$ by one unit while holding $y_{t-1}$, every disturbance, and
every other intervention fixed. Derive the causal response $\theta_h$.

(c) For the population regression of $y_{t+h}$ on $(1,s_t,y_{t-1})$, read off
$\mu_h$, $\beta_h$, $\gamma_h$, and the residual $u_{t,h}$ from your formula.
Show that $\mathbb E[u_{t,h}]=\mathbb E[s_tu_{t,h}]=\mathbb E[y_{t-1}u_{t,h}]=0$,
and name the assumption each step uses.

(d) With $\theta_0=1$ and $\rho=0.9$, compute $\theta_4$ and $\theta_7$, and find
the first horizon at which the response is below half of its impact value.
:::

:::: {.solution-material}
::: {.callout-tip .exercise-hint collapse="true" icon=false}
## Hint

Do two substitutions by hand before writing any sum, and watch what the second
substitution does to every term the first one produced. That operation is the
induction step. For (c), write down the date of every term in $u_{t,h}$ before
taking a single expectation.
:::

::: {.callout-note .exercise-solution collapse="true" icon=false}
## Detailed solution

The object we want is $y_{t+h}$ written as "the pre-intervention outcome, plus
everything that arrives from $t$ onward." The rule gives each outcome in terms
of the previous one, so we replace the previous outcome repeatedly until only
$y_{t-1}$ is left.

**(a)** At $h=0$ the rule itself is already in that form. For $h=1$, write the
rule one period later and substitute for $y_t$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y_{t+1}&=\rho\,y_t+\theta_0s_{t+1}+v_{t+1}\\
&=\rho\bigl(\rho\,y_{t-1}+\theta_0s_t+v_t\bigr)+\theta_0s_{t+1}+v_{t+1}\\
&=\rho^2y_{t-1}+\rho\,\theta_0s_t+\rho\,v_t+\theta_0s_{t+1}+v_{t+1}.
\end{aligned}
$$

For $h=2$, write $y_{t+2}=\rho\,y_{t+1}+\theta_0s_{t+2}+v_{t+2}$ and substitute
the last line:

$$
y_{t+2}=\rho^3y_{t-1}+\rho^2\theta_0s_t+\rho^2v_t+\rho\,\theta_0s_{t+1}
+\rho\,v_{t+1}+\theta_0s_{t+2}+v_{t+2}.
$$

The second substitution multiplied every existing term by $\rho$ and appended
the new period's intervention and disturbance with coefficient one. Repeating
that operation suggests

$$
y_{t+h}=\rho^{h+1}y_{t-1}+\sum_{j=0}^{h}\rho^{h-j}\bigl(\theta_0s_{t+j}+v_{t+j}\bigr).
$$

*Induction.* At $h=0$ the formula reads $\rho\,y_{t-1}+\theta_0s_t+v_t$, which is
the rule. Suppose it holds at $h$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
y_{t+h+1}&=\rho\,y_{t+h}+\theta_0s_{t+h+1}+v_{t+h+1}\\
&=\rho^{h+2}y_{t-1}+\sum_{j=0}^{h}\rho^{h+1-j}\bigl(\theta_0s_{t+j}+v_{t+j}\bigr)
+\rho^{0}\bigl(\theta_0s_{t+h+1}+v_{t+h+1}\bigr),
\end{aligned}
$$

and the last term is the $j=h+1$ term of the sum at horizon $h+1$. The formula
therefore holds at $h+1$, and so at every horizon.

**(b)** The intervention $s_t$ appears only in the $j=0$ term of the sum, with
coefficient $\rho^h\theta_0$. Raising $s_t$ by one unit with everything else
fixed raises $y_{t+h}$ by that coefficient, so

$$
\theta_h=\theta_0\rho^h,
$$

in units of $y$ per unit of $s$. The rule is linear and its coefficients do not
depend on the date (A1), so the response is the same for every $t$ and for any
starting value of $s_t$.

**(c)** Match the formula with $y_{t+h}=\mu_h+\beta_hs_t+\gamma_hy_{t-1}+u_{t,h}$.
The proposal is $\mu_h=0$, $\beta_h=\theta_0\rho^h$, $\gamma_h=\rho^{h+1}$, and
everything left over is the residual:

$$
u_{t,h}=\sum_{j=0}^{h}\rho^{h-j}v_{t+j}+\theta_0\sum_{j=1}^{h}\rho^{h-j}s_{t+j}.
$$

Its terms are dated as follows: the disturbances $v_t,\dots,v_{t+h}$ and the
interventions $s_{t+1},\dots,s_{t+h}$. The second sum starts at $j=1$ because
$s_t$ has moved into the $\beta_h$ term. A proposal is the population projection
if its residual satisfies the three orthogonality conditions, because only one
set of coefficients does when $s_t$ and $y_{t-1}$ both vary and neither is an
exact linear function of the other. Here $\sigma_s^2>0$ (A2), and $y_{t-1}$,
built from terms dated $t-1$ or earlier, varies and is uncorrelated with $s_t$
(A2, A3).

1. *Mean zero.* Every $v_{t+j}$ and every $s_{t+j}$ has mean zero (A2, A3), so
   $\mathbb E[u_{t,h}]=0$.
2. *Orthogonal to $s_t$.* The product $s_tu_{t,h}$ is a sum of terms
   $s_tv_{t+j}$ with $j\ge0$ and $s_ts_{t+j}$ with $j\ge1$. The first kind has
   expectation $\mathbb E[s_t]\,\mathbb E[v_{t+j}]=0$ because the two sequences
   are independent (A3). The second kind has expectation
   $\mathbb E[s_t]\,\mathbb E[s_{t+j}]=0$ because interventions are independent
   over time with mean zero (A2).
3. *Orthogonal to $y_{t-1}$.* Iterating the rule backward,
   $y_{t-1}=\sum_{i\ge0}\rho^i(\theta_0s_{t-1-i}+v_{t-1-i})$, a sum that settles
   down because $|\rho|<1$ (A4). Every term of $y_{t-1}$ is dated $t-1$ or
   earlier, every term of $u_{t,h}$ is dated $t$ or later, and by A2 and A3 the
   two groups are independent. Each term of $u_{t,h}$ has mean zero, so
   $\mathbb E[y_{t-1}u_{t,h}]=0$.

All three conditions hold, so the projection coefficients are
$\mu_h=0$, $\beta_h=\theta_h=\theta_0\rho^h$, and $\gamma_h=\rho^{h+1}$. As a
special-case check, at $h=0$ the residual is $u_{t,0}=v_t$, $\beta_0=\theta_0$,
and $\gamma_0=\rho$: the projection is the rule itself.

Two of the three steps used the assumptions about how interventions and
disturbances arise, and none used anything about least squares. That is where
the causal content of $\beta_h=\theta_h$ sits.

**(d)** With $\theta_0=1$ and $\rho=0.9$,

$$
\theta_4=0.9^4=0.6561,
\qquad
\theta_7=0.9^7=0.4782969.
$$

The response falls below half of its impact value when $0.9^h<0.5$, that is,
when $h>\ln0.5/\ln0.9=6.58$ (rounded to two decimals). The first such horizon is
$h=7$; one period earlier, $\theta_6=0.531441$ is still above one half. The
control's coefficient over the same horizons is $\gamma_h=0.9^{h+1}$, for
example $\gamma_4=0.59049$, but it measures the fading of the pre-intervention
outcome, not a response to anything.

Three slips recur. Starting the intervention sum in $u_{t,h}$ at $j=0$ puts
$s_t$ into the residual, which makes $\mathbb E[s_tu_{t,h}]=\theta_0\rho^h\sigma_s^2$
and suggests a bias that does not exist. Writing $\gamma_h=\rho^h$ forgets that
$y_{t-1}$ has had $h+1$ periods to fade. And attributing
$\mathbb E[y_{t-1}u_{t,h}]=0$ to A2 alone overlooks that $y_{t-1}$ contains past
disturbances, so A3 is needed as well.
:::
::::

### Exercise 3: Rows by hand {.unnumbered .exercise-title #exercise-l01-3}

::: {.exercise}
**Problem.** [core, pencil] In the twelve-period economy the interventions are
$s_t=1$ at $t=1,5,10,12$ and $s_t=0$ otherwise, and the realized outcomes are

| $t$ | $y_t$ | $t$ | $y_t$ | $t$ | $y_t$ |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 1.9 | 5 | −0.66875 | 9 | 0.658203125 |
| 2 | 1.45 | 6 | −0.134375 | 10 | 1.9291015625 |
| 3 | 1.325 | 7 | 2.0328125 | 11 | 0.06455078125 |
| 4 | 0.0625 | 8 | −0.28359375 | 12 | 2.532275390625 |

For $h=0,1,2$, consider the regression of $y_{t+h}$ on a constant and $s_t$,
using only rows with $t\ge2$ so that $y_{t-1}$ would exist in every row.

(a) List the rows of each regression and give $T_h$. Check your count against
$T_h=T-h-p$.

(b) Identify the intervention rows and compute the mean of $y_{t+h}$ over the
intervention rows, $\bar y_1$, and over the other rows, $\bar y_0$.

(c) Compute $\hat\beta_h$ and compare it with $\theta_h=0.5^h$.

(d) Row 4 of the $h=1$ regression sits in the comparison group. What is its
outcome, and why is that outcome not a clean comparison?
:::

:::: {.solution-material}
::: {.callout-tip .exercise-hint collapse="true" icon=false}
## Hint

Draw the staircase before computing anything. For each $h$, write $t$ in one
column and $t+h$ in the next, then strike out every row whose outcome date
passes 12. Only after that sort the surviving rows by $s_t$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .exercise-solution collapse="true" icon=false}
## Detailed solution

A regression row is dated by its intervention: row $t$ pairs $s_t$ with the
outcome $y_{t+h}$. Row $t$ needs the lag $y_{t-1}$, which exists only for $t\ge2$
because $y_0$ is not part of the data, and the lead $y_{t+h}$, which exists
only for $t\le12-h$. The plan is to fix those rows first, then use the fact
from the notes that with a 0–1 regressor the least-squares slope is the
difference in means, $\hat\beta_h=\bar y_1-\bar y_0$.

**(a)** The rows are $t=2,\dots,12$ at $h=0$, $t=2,\dots,11$ at $h=1$, and
$t=2,\dots,10$ at $h=2$, so $T_0=11$, $T_1=10$, and $T_2=9$. With $T=12$ and one
lag, $p=1$, the formula gives $T_h=12-h-1$: 11, 10, and 9. Each horizon costs
the last row, and the lag costs row 1 at every horizon.

**(b)** At $h=0$ the intervention rows are 5, 10, and 12. At $h=1$ row 12 has
left the sample, because its outcome $y_{13}$ does not exist, and the
intervention rows are 5 and 10; they remain 5 and 10 at $h=2$. Each row
contributes its outcome $h$ periods later:

- $h=0$. Intervention outcomes $y_5,y_{10},y_{12}$ sum to $3.792626953125$, so
  $\bar y_1=1.264208984375$. The eight other outcomes $y_2,y_3,y_4,y_6,y_7,y_8,y_9,y_{11}$
  sum to $5.17509765625$, so $\bar y_0=0.64688720703125$.
- $h=1$. Intervention outcomes $y_6$ and $y_{11}$ sum to $-0.06982421875$, so
  $\bar y_1=-0.034912109375$. The eight other rows $t=2,3,4,6,7,8,9,11$ have
  outcomes $y_3,y_4,y_5,y_7,y_8,y_9,y_{10},y_{12}$, which sum to
  $7.587548828125$, so $\bar y_0=0.948443603515625$.
- $h=2$. Intervention outcomes $y_7$ and $y_{12}$ sum to $4.565087890625$, so
  $\bar y_1=2.2825439453125$. The seven other rows $t=2,3,4,6,7,8,9$ have
  outcomes $y_4,y_5,y_6,y_8,y_9,y_{10},y_{11}$, which sum to $1.62763671875$,
  so $\bar y_0=0.23251953125$.

**(c)** Subtracting,

$$
\hat\beta_0=0.61732177734375,\qquad
\hat\beta_1=-0.983355712890625,\qquad
\hat\beta_2=2.0500244140625.
$$

| $h$ | $T_h$ | Rows | Intervention rows | $\bar y_1$ | $\bar y_0$ | $\hat\beta_h$ | $\theta_h$ |
|---:|---:|:---:|:---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 11 | 2–12 | 5, 10, 12 | 1.264209 | 0.646887 | 0.617322 | 1 |
| 1 | 10 | 2–11 | 5, 10 | −0.034912 | 0.948444 | −0.983356 | 0.5 |
| 2 | 9 | 2–10 | 5, 10 | 2.282544 | 0.232520 | 2.050024 | 0.25 |

The table rounds to six decimals; the display above it is exact. The slopes
are in units of $y$ per unit of $s$. None is close to its target: the impact
estimate is 0.62 against 1, the $h=1$ estimate has the wrong sign, and the
$h=2$ estimate is eight times too large. Two or three intervention rows cannot
average away disturbances such as $v_5=-1.7$ and $v_7=2.1$.

*Check.* The covariance form of the slope must agree. At $h=0$, $\bar s=3/11$,
so $\sum_t(s_t-\bar s)^2=n_1n_0/n=3\times8/11=24/11$, and
$\sum_t(s_t-\bar s)\,y_t=1.346883877841$ (rounded to twelve decimals). Their
ratio is $0.617321777\ldots$, the same slope. The intercept of each
regression equals $\bar y_0$, which is a second check.

**(d)** Row 4 has $s_4=0$, so it belongs to the comparison group, but its
outcome at $h=1$ is $y_5=0.5\,y_4+s_5+v_5=-0.66875$, which contains the
intervention at $t=5$. In the notation of the notes this is the term
$\theta_0s_{t+1}$ inside the residual $u_{t,1}$. Rows 9 and 11 have the same
feature: their outcomes $y_{10}$ and $y_{12}$ contain the interventions at
$t=10$ and $t=12$, while neither intervention row has an intervention one
period later. Through that term alone, the comparison mean $\bar y_0$ carries
three units of intervention spread over eight rows, which adds $3/8=0.375$ to
$\bar y_0$ and lowers $\hat\beta_1$ by the same amount. In population this does
no harm, because $s_{t+1}$ is independent of $s_t$ and averages out across many
rows. In ten rows it does not average out.

The most common slip is to compute $\bar y_1$ minus the mean of *all* rows
instead of the mean of the other rows. That gives
$(n_0/n)(\bar y_1-\bar y_0)=(8/11)\times0.61732177734375=0.448961\ldots$ at
$h=0$. Another is to leave row 12 in the $h=1$ regression with a blank outcome
treated as zero, which adds a fictitious intervention row.
:::
::::

### Exercise 4: The same rows in Stata {.unnumbered .exercise-title #exercise-l01-4}

::: {.exercise}
**Problem.** [core, computational] Reproduce the regressions of
[Exercise 3](#exercise-l01-3) in Stata, then add the lagged outcome as a control
on the same rows. Write a do-file that

(a) enters the twelve rows of the hand table (the values of $s_t$ and $v_t$
are $s_t=1$ at $t=1,5,10,12$ and
$v_t=0.9,\,0.5,\,0.6,\,-0.6,\,-1.7,\,0.2,\,2.1,\,-1.3,\,0.8,\,0.6,\,-0.9,\,1.5$),
rebuilds $y_t$ from $y_t=0.5\,y_{t-1}+s_t+v_t$ with $y_0=0$, and declares the
data with `tsset t`;

(b) loops over $h=0,1,2$ with `forvalues`, computes $\bar y_1$ and $\bar y_0$
with `summarize`, and runs ``regress F`h'.y s if t >= 2`` with and without
`L.y`, storing $h$, $T_h$, and both slopes;

(c) asserts that $T_h=11-h$ in both regressions, that the slope without the
control equals $\bar y_1-\bar y_0$ to within $10^{-6}$, that both regressions
use exactly the same rows, and that the slopes without the control equal those
of Exercise 3.

Report the three slopes with the control and explain why they are no longer
differences in means.
:::

:::: {.solution-material}
::: {.callout-tip .exercise-hint collapse="true" icon=false}
## Hint

Check `e(N)` before you look at any coefficient. Stata's `F.` operator returns
a missing value past the last period and `regress` drops such rows without
comment, so the row count is the first thing that can go wrong. Ask, too,
which rows the regression with `L.y` loses that the one without it keeps.
:::

::: {.callout-note .exercise-solution collapse="true" icon=false}
## Detailed solution

The do-file below types the rows rather than drawing them, so it depends on
neither a data file nor a random-number stream. It stores $v_t$ and $y_t$ as
`double`, for a reason given at the end. The assertions sit where the claims of
Exercise 3 are made: the row count right after each regression, the
difference in means before the slope is stored, and the comparison of samples
before the control's slope is posted.

```stata
* ex04_hand_rows.do  Lecture 01, Exercise 4: the hand-table rows in Stata
* Run from the lab project's top folder with StataNow/SE 19.5.
version 19
clear all
set more off
capture log close
log using output/ex04_hand_rows.txt, text replace

* The twelve rows of the hand table, typed from the notes. Storing v and y
* as double keeps Stata's arithmetic equal to the exact decimals.
input byte t byte s double v
 1 1  0.9
 2 0  0.5
 3 0  0.6
 4 0 -0.6
 5 1 -1.7
 6 0  0.2
 7 0  2.1
 8 0 -1.3
 9 0  0.8
10 1  0.6
11 0 -0.9
12 1  1.5
end
tsset t
generate double y = s + v in 1                  // y_0 = 0
replace y = 0.5*L.y + s + v in 2/12
assert abs(y[5]  - (-0.66875))     < 1e-12   // check the typed rows
assert abs(y[12] - 2.532275390625) < 1e-12

tempname P
postfile `P' h T_h n1 n0 double(ybar1 ybar0 b_noctrl b_ctrl) ///
    using output/ex04_results, replace
forvalues h = 0/2 {
    * group means of the outcome h periods ahead, rows t >= 2
    quietly summarize F`h'.y if t >= 2 & s == 1
    local ybar1 = r(mean)
    local n1 = r(N)
    quietly summarize F`h'.y if t >= 2 & s == 0
    local ybar0 = r(mean)
    local n0 = r(N)

    * the regression without the control
    quietly regress F`h'.y s if t >= 2
    assert e(N) == 11 - `h'                     // T_h = T - h - p
    assert `n1' + `n0' == e(N)
    assert abs(_b[s] - (`ybar1' - `ybar0')) < 1e-6
    assert abs(_b[_cons] - `ybar0') < 1e-6
    local b_noctrl = _b[s]
    tempvar rows
    generate byte `rows' = e(sample)

    * the regression with y_(t-1), which must use the same rows
    quietly regress F`h'.y s L.y if t >= 2
    assert e(N) == 11 - `h'
    quietly count if e(sample) != `rows'
    assert r(N) == 0
    post `P' (`h') (e(N)) (`n1') (`n0') (`ybar1') (`ybar0') ///
        (`b_noctrl') (_b[s])
    drop `rows'
}
postclose `P'

use output/ex04_results, clear
format ybar1 ybar0 b_noctrl b_ctrl %12.8f
list, clean noobs

* exact slopes from the notes; with-control slopes to six decimals
assert n1 == cond(h == 0, 3, 2)
assert abs(b_noctrl - 0.61732177734375)     < 1e-9 if h == 0
assert abs(b_noctrl - (-0.983355712890625)) < 1e-9 if h == 1
assert abs(b_noctrl - 2.0500244140625)      < 1e-9 if h == 2
assert abs(b_ctrl - 0.575667)    < 5e-7 if h == 0
assert abs(b_ctrl - (-1.050405)) < 5e-7 if h == 1
assert abs(b_ctrl - 2.153022)    < 5e-7 if h == 2
display "Exercise 4: all assertions passed"
log close
```

Run in StataNow/SE 19.5, every assertion passes. The listing in the log is:

```text
    h   T_h   n1   n0         ybar1        ybar0      b_noctrl        b_ctrl
    0    11    3    8    1.26420898   0.64688721    0.61732178    0.57566739
    1    10    2    8   -0.03491211   0.94844360   -0.98335571   -1.05040519
    2     9    2    7    2.28254395   0.23251953    2.05002441    2.15302246
```

Without the control, each slope is the difference in means of Exercise 3,
printed to eight decimals: 0.61732178 is 0.61732177734375 rounded. The row
counts confirm $T_h=T-h-p$, and the group sizes confirm that row 12's
intervention leaves at $h=1$.

With $y_{t-1}$ included, the slopes are 0.575667, $-1.050405$, and 2.153022
(rounded to six decimals), on exactly the same rows. They are no longer
differences in means. By the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell result that the notes preview
in a footnote, the slope now uses $s_t$ after removing its linear relation to
$y_{t-1}$ in these rows. In population that relation is zero, because the
intervention is independent of the previous outcome (A2 and A3). In nine to
eleven rows it is not exactly zero, so the control moves the three estimates by
0.04, 0.07, and 0.10 in absolute value (rounded to two decimals). The control's own
coefficients tell the same story: exact least squares on these rows gives
$\hat\gamma_0=-0.061$, $\hat\gamma_1=-0.115$, and $\hat\gamma_2=0.233$ (rounded
to three decimals), against $\rho^{h+1}=0.5$, 0.25, and 0.125. The population
coefficient the two regressions target is the same, $\beta_h=\theta_h$; neither
estimate comes near it in twelve periods.

*Why the tolerance.* With `double` storage, Stata's slopes agree with exact
decimal arithmetic to about $10^{-15}$, so even the $10^{-9}$ assertions pass.
Stored as `float`, which is what `generate` and `input` use by default, $v_t$
becomes a binary approximation such as 0.89999998; delete `double` from the
`input` and `generate` lines to see it. The slopes then print as 0.61732179,
$-0.98335569$, and 2.05002437, the values the notes quote, because the shipped
`hand_table.csv` was generated from float draws. They still satisfy every
$10^{-6}$ assertion, while the $10^{-12}$ checks on the typed rows and the
$10^{-9}$ checks on the slopes fail, as they should. A test written as
`assert _b[s] == ybar1 - ybar0` would be testing storage, not the regression.

*What the first assertion catches.* Leaving out `if t >= 2` changes one regression but not
the other. At $h=0$ the regression without the control then uses all twelve
rows, including row 1 with its intervention, and returns $0.7762695$ (rounded
to seven decimals). The regression with `L.y` still uses eleven rows, because
$y_0$ is missing. The two slopes would differ in their rows as well as in their
control, and the first assertion, `e(N) == 11 - h`, stops the do-file before
anyone compares them.
:::
::::

### Exercise 5: One episode {.unnumbered .exercise-title #exercise-l01-5}

::: {.exercise}
**Problem.** [core, pencil] Replace the intervention column of the hand table
by an indicator that equals 1 at $t=5$ and 0 at every other date, and keep the
rows $t\ge2$ and the outcomes listed in [Exercise 3](#exercise-l01-3).

(a) Show that when exactly one of $n$ rows, row $\tau$, has the indicator equal
to 1, the least-squares slope of $y_{t+h}$ on a constant and the indicator is
$y_{\tau+h}-\bar y_{\text{others}}$, where $\bar y_{\text{others}}$ is the mean
outcome over the other $n-1$ rows.

(b) Compute the slope at $h=0,1,2$ and compare each with $\theta_h=0.5^h$.

(c) Use the forward equation $y_{\tau+h}=\theta_h+\rho^{h+1}y_{\tau-1}+u_{\tau,h}$
to split the $h=0$ slope into $\theta_0$ and everything else. Which term
dominates?

(d) Return to the original intervention column ($s_t=1$ at $t=1,5,10,12$). As
$h$ grows, the regression of $y_{t+h}$ on $s_t$ over rows $t\ge2$ becomes a
single-episode regression without any change to the data. At which horizon
does that first happen, and what is the slope there?
:::

:::: {.solution-material}
::: {.callout-tip .exercise-hint collapse="true" icon=false}
## Hint

With a single intervention row, the "mean of the intervention rows" is one
outcome. Start from the difference-in-means result of Exercise 3 with $n_1=1$,
or compute $\bar s$, $\sum_t(s_t-\bar s)^2$, and the weight on each row
directly.
:::

::: {.callout-note .exercise-solution collapse="true" icon=false}
## Detailed solution

**(a)** The slope on a 0–1 regressor is the difference in means, so with one
intervention row $\bar y_1=y_{\tau+h}$ and $\bar y_0=\bar y_{\text{others}}$,
and the result follows at once. The weights make the same point more
concretely. With one intervention among $n$ rows, $\bar s=1/n$ and

$$
\sum_t(s_t-\bar s)^2=\Bigl(1-\frac1n\Bigr)^2+(n-1)\frac{1}{n^2}
=\frac{(n-1)^2+(n-1)}{n^2}=\frac{n-1}{n}.
$$

The slope is $\sum_t\omega_ty_{t+h}$ with $\omega_t=(s_t-\bar s)/\sum_\tau(s_\tau-\bar s)^2$.
Row $\tau$ gets $\omega_\tau=(1-1/n)\big/\bigl((n-1)/n\bigr)=1$, and every other
row gets $-(1/n)\big/\bigl((n-1)/n\bigr)=-1/(n-1)$. Hence

$$
\hat\beta_h=y_{\tau+h}-\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{t\neq\tau}y_{t+h}
=y_{\tau+h}-\bar y_{\text{others}}.
$$

The episode's outcome gets full weight, and the other rows share a weight of
$-1$ equally.

**(b)** At $h=0$ the rows are $t=2,\dots,12$, so $n=11$. The episode's outcome is
$y_5=-0.66875$, and the ten other outcomes sum to $9.636474609375$, a mean of
$0.9636474609375$. At $h=1$ ($n=10$) the episode's outcome is $y_6=-0.134375$,
and the nine others, $y_3,y_4,y_5,y_7,\dots,y_{12}$, sum to $7.652099609375$,
a mean of $0.850233289\ldots$. At $h=2$ ($n=9$) the episode's outcome is
$y_7=2.0328125$, and the eight others, $y_4,y_5,y_6,y_8,\dots,y_{12}$, sum to
$4.159912109375$, a mean of $0.519989013671875$. So

$$
\hat\beta_0=-1.6323974609375,\qquad
\hat\beta_1=-0.984608\ldots,\qquad
\hat\beta_2=1.512823486328125,
$$

or $-1.632397$, $-0.984608$, and $1.512823$ rounded to six decimals, against
$\theta_h=1$, 0.5, and 0.25. Two estimates have the wrong sign and the third is
six times too large.

**(c)** At $\tau=5$ and $h=0$ the forward equation is the rule itself:
$y_5=\theta_0+\rho\,y_4+u_{5,0}$ with $u_{5,0}=v_5$. Substituting $\theta_0=1$,
$\rho\,y_4=0.5\times0.0625=0.03125$, and $v_5=-1.7$,

$$
\hat\beta_0=\underbrace{1}_{\theta_0}
+\underbrace{\bigl(0.03125-1.7-0.9636474609375\bigr)}_{\text{everything else}}
=1+(-2.6323974609375)=-1.6323974609375.
$$

Everything else is more than twice the response, and the episode's own
disturbance, $-1.7$, is by itself larger than $\theta_0$. The same split works at
$h=1$: $y_6=\theta_1+\rho^2y_4+u_{5,1}$ with
$u_{5,1}=\rho\,v_5+v_6+\theta_0s_6=-0.85+0.2+0=-0.65$, so
$\hat\beta_1=0.5+(0.015625-0.65-0.850233\ldots)=0.5+(-1.484608\ldots)$.
The data contain one number at each horizon. Nothing in them says how much of it
is $\theta_h$ and how much is the bracket.

**(d)** At $h=3$ the rows are $t=2,\dots,9$. Row 10 and row 12 have no outcome
three periods later, and row 1 is excluded, so row 5 is the only intervention
row left. The original regression is then exactly the single-episode
regression, and part (a) applies to it unchanged:

$$
\hat\beta_3=y_8-\frac{y_5+y_6+y_7+y_9+y_{10}+y_{11}+y_{12}}{7}
=-0.28359375-\frac{6.413818359375}{7}=-1.199853515625,
$$

against $\theta_3=0.125$. This is also a check on (a): the slope from the
difference-in-means formula of Exercise 3 and the slope from the one-episode
formula must coincide here, and they do. Row 5 stays the only intervention row
through $h=7$, so the regressions at $h=4,\dots,7$, on 7, 6, 5, and 4 rows, are
single-episode regressions as well. At $h=8$ the rows are $t=2,3,4$, none of
them has an intervention, $s_t$ does not vary, and no slope can be computed;
Stata's `regress` reports `s` as omitted because of collinearity.

The Korean episode in the notes has the same structure, with taxes, the
Treasury–Federal Reserve Accord, and price controls inside the bracket.

It is easy to subtract the mean of all $n$ rows, including the
episode itself. That shrinks the answer by the factor $(n-1)/n$: at $h=0$ it
gives $(10/11)\times(-1.6323974609375)=-1.483998$ (rounded to six decimals).
The error is small here, but it hides the logic of the formula, which compares
the episode with everything else.
:::
::::

### Exercise 6: A response in a loop {.unnumbered .exercise-title #exercise-l01-6}

::: {.exercise}
**Problem.** [core, computational] The Practicum 01 lab project ships
`data/raw/onedraw_rho09_seed2.csv`, one simulated sample of $T=200$ periods
from $y_t=0.9\,y_{t-1}+s_t+v_t$ with $\sigma_s=\sigma_v=1$ (seed 2; variables
`t`, `s`, `v`, `y`). Lab 3 of the Shock-to-Response Explorer displays the same
observations.

(a) Write a do-file that loops over $h=0,\dots,12$, regresses $y_{t+h}$ on a
constant, $s_t$, and $y_{t-1}$, and stores $h$, $\hat\beta_h$, and $T_h$ with
`postfile`.

(b) Assert that $T_h=199-h$, that $\hat\beta_0=0.878940$ and
$\hat\beta_{12}=-0.293297$ to within $10^{-6}$, and state how many of the
thirteen estimates lie below $\theta_h=0.9^h$.

(c) Draw the response graph with $\theta_h$ overlaid and write a caption that
names the intervention and its units, the units of the outcome, the horizon
unit, and the counterfactual.

(d) In two or three sentences, say what the graph shows about this sample and
what it cannot show.
:::

:::: {.solution-material}
::: {.callout-tip .exercise-hint collapse="true" icon=false}
## Hint

Put `e(N)` in the same `post` command as `_b[s]`, so each coefficient travels
with the number of rows behind it. For the caption, fill four slots before
writing a sentence: what one unit of the intervention is, what the vertical
axis measures, what the horizontal axis counts, and what a value of zero is
being compared with.
:::

::: {.callout-note .exercise-solution collapse="true" icon=false}
## Detailed solution

One regression per horizon produces one point on the curve, so the loop has
thirteen regressions and a results file with thirteen rows. The design
decision that matters most is to store each coefficient together with its sample
size and to test the sample size before trusting the coefficient.

```stata
* ex06_loop.do  Lecture 01, Exercise 6: a response in a loop
* Run from the lab project's top folder with StataNow/SE 19.5.
version 19
clear all
set more off
capture log close
log using output/ex06_loop.txt, text replace

import delimited using data/raw/onedraw_rho09_seed2.csv, clear   // t s v y
tsset t
assert _N == 200

tempname P
postfile `P' h double beta_h T_h using output/results_onedraw, replace
forvalues h = 0/12 {
    quietly regress F`h'.y s L.y
    post `P' (`h') (_b[s]) (e(N))          // coefficient with its rows
}
postclose `P'

use output/results_onedraw, clear
generate double theta_h = 0.9^h
assert T_h == 199 - h                        // T - h - p, T = 200, p = 1
assert abs(beta_h[1]  - 0.878940)    < 1e-6  // h = 0
assert abs(beta_h[13] - (-0.293297)) < 1e-6  // h = 12
quietly count if beta_h < theta_h
assert r(N) == 13                            // below the truth at every h
format beta_h theta_h %9.6f
list h T_h beta_h theta_h, clean noobs

twoway (line theta_h h, lcolor(gs8) lpattern(dash))                  ///
       (connected beta_h h, lcolor(navy) mcolor(navy) msize(small)), ///
       yline(0, lcolor(gs13))                                        ///
       xlabel(0(2)12) ylabel(-0.4(0.2)1, format(%3.1f) angle(0))     ///
       xtitle("Horizon h (periods after the intervention)")          ///
       ytitle("Gap from the no-intervention path (units of y)")      ///
       legend(order(2 "Estimate, this sample"                        ///
                    1 "True response 0.9{sup:h}") rows(1) position(6)) ///
       graphregion(color(white)) plotregion(color(white))
graph export output/ex06_response.pdf, replace
display "Exercise 6: all assertions passed"
log close
```

The assertions pass, and the log lists:

```text
     h   T_h      beta_h    theta_h
     0   199    0.878940   1.000000
     1   198    0.853260   0.900000
     2   197    0.612737   0.810000
     3   196    0.611046   0.729000
     4   195    0.548477   0.656100
     5   194    0.583099   0.590490
     6   193    0.509120   0.531441
     7   192    0.417788   0.478297
     8   191    0.240595   0.430467
     9   190    0.130293   0.387420
    10   189   -0.028821   0.348678
    11   188   -0.117200   0.313811
    12   187   -0.293297   0.282430
```

An independent least-squares calculation in Python on the same CSV reproduces
all thirteen coefficients to the six decimals shown. All thirteen estimates lie
below $\theta_h$. In the exported graph the connected estimate starts near
0.88 and runs below the dashed truth by between 0.01 and 0.20 through $h=8$
(rounded to two decimals). After that the gap widens at every step, and the
estimate is negative from $h=10$ on while $0.9^h$ stays positive.

*A caption that does its job.* "Response of $y$ to a one-unit intervention
$s_t$ (one unit is one standard deviation, since $\sigma_s=1$), estimated by
local projections of $y_{t+h}$ on a constant, $s_t$, and $y_{t-1}$ in one
simulated sample of $T=200$ periods with $\rho=0.9$ (seed 2). Horizons are
periods after the intervention; $h=0$ is the period in which it occurs. The
vertical axis is the gap between the path with the intervention and the path
without it, in units of $y$. The dashed line is the true response
$\theta_h=0.9^h$. No sampling uncertainty is shown." Each of the four slots is
filled: the intervention and its unit, the outcome's units, the horizon unit,
and the counterfactual that zero refers to.

*What the graph shows and what it does not.* In this sample the estimated
response is below the truth at every horizon. The shortfall grows from 0.19 at
$h=8$ to 0.58 at $h=12$ (rounded to two decimals), and a reader shown only this
curve would say the effect turns negative at $h=10$. The
graph cannot say whether the sample is typical. Neighbouring estimates share
almost all their rows and most of their residual terms, so a curve that errs
in one direction at every horizon may be one error seen thirteen times. Only
the distribution across many samples, which [Exercise 7](#exercise-l01-7)
builds, or a band computed from the sample itself, which Lectures 5 and 6
build, can separate the two.

The mistake to expect here is in the caption rather than the code. Writing
"response of $y$" on the vertical axis without saying that zero means "no
different from the path without the intervention" invites the reading that
zero means "$y$ is back where it started". The graph measures gaps between
paths, not changes along one.
:::
::::

### Exercise 7: Many draws {.unnumbered .exercise-title #exercise-l01-7}

::: {.exercise}
**Problem.** [computational] Wrap the loop of [Exercise 6](#exercise-l01-6) in
a Monte Carlo experiment. Each sample comes from $y_t=\rho\,y_{t-1}+s_t+v_t$
with $y_0=0$ and $s_t$ and $v_t$ independent standard normal draws: 300
periods, all 300 values of $s$ drawn before any $v$ (`generate s = rnormal()`,
then `generate v = rnormal()`), the first 100 periods discarded, so $T=200$.
Set the seed to 3 once for each $\rho\in\{0.5,0.9\}$, outside the replication
loop, and expose the number of replications as `global R` with a default of
200. In each sample, estimate $\hat\beta_h$ for $h=0,\dots,12$ with $y_{t-1}$
($199-h$ rows) and without it, on every row that has the lead ($200-h$ rows).

(a) For each $\rho$ and $h$, report the mean, standard deviation, and 5th and
95th percentiles of $\hat\beta_h$ with the control, and the mean and standard
deviation without it. With $R=200$, assert that at $\rho=0.9$ and $h=8$ the mean
and standard deviation with the control are 0.370337 and 0.211226 to within
$10^{-6}$.

(b) Using the Monte Carlo standard error, the standard deviation divided by
$\sqrt R$, decide at which horizons the mean differs from $\theta_h=\rho^h$ by
more than simulation noise.

(c) Compare the spread with and without the control at each $\rho$. Explain the
pattern with the variance of the term $\rho^{h+1}y_{t-1}$ that the regression
without the control leaves in its residual.

(d) Where does the sample of Exercise 6 lie relative to the 5–95 percent band at
$h=8$ and at $h=12$?
:::

:::: {.solution-material}
::: {.callout-tip .exercise-hint collapse="true" icon=false}
## Hint

Post every estimate with its replication number, $\rho$, $h$, and `e(N)`, and
compute summaries after the loop from the stored estimates rather than inside
it. For (c), work out $\rho^{2(h+1)}\operatorname{Var}(y)$ at $h=0$ and $h=4$
for both values of $\rho$ before you look at the simulated standard deviations.
:::

::: {.callout-note .exercise-solution collapse="true" icon=false}
## Detailed solution

<!-- D2: global R, student default 200. D26 and D53: two runs of the do-file below took 27.3
     and 27.8 seconds at R = 200 in StataNow/SE 19.5, so the exercise is not
     [extra]. -->

A Monte Carlo experiment answers a question one sample cannot: how an estimator
behaves when the true response is known. The design fixes everything except
the draws, so differences across replications are sampling variation and
differences between the mean and $\theta_h$ are properties of the estimator.
Seeding once per design makes the $R=200$ run the first 200 replications of the
same stream as the notes' $R=500$ table.

```stata
* ex07_many_draws.do  Lecture 01, Exercise 7: many draws
* Run from the lab project's top folder with StataNow/SE 19.5.
version 19
clear all
set more off
capture log close
log using output/ex07_many_draws.txt, text replace

if "$R" == "" global R 200          // replications (D2 student default)
timer clear 1
timer on 1

tempname P
postfile `P' rep double rho h double(b_ctrl b_noctrl) n_ctrl n_noctrl ///
    using output/mc_draws, replace
foreach rho in 0.5 0.9 {
    set seed 3                      // once per design, before the loop
    quietly forvalues r = 1/$R {
        clear
        set obs 300
        generate t = _n
        tsset t
        generate s = rnormal()                  // s first, then v
        generate v = rnormal()
        generate y = s + v in 1
        replace y = `rho'*L.y + s + v in 2/300
        drop if t <= 100                        // burn-in of 100 periods
        replace t = _n
        tsset t
        forvalues h = 0/12 {
            regress F`h'.y s L.y
            local b_c = _b[s]
            local n_c = e(N)
            regress F`h'.y s
            post `P' (`r') (`rho') (`h') (`b_c') (_b[s]) (`n_c') (e(N))
        }
    }
}
postclose `P'
timer off 1
quietly timer list 1
display "Monte Carlo runtime: " %6.1f r(t1) " seconds for R = $R"

use output/mc_draws, clear
assert n_ctrl == 199 - h & n_noctrl == 200 - h
generate double theta_h = rho^h
collapse (mean) theta_h mean_ctrl=b_ctrl mean_noctrl=b_noctrl ///
         (sd) sd_ctrl=b_ctrl sd_noctrl=b_noctrl               ///
         (p5) p5=b_ctrl (p95) p95=b_ctrl, by(rho h)
generate double bias = mean_ctrl - theta_h
generate double mcse = sd_ctrl/sqrt($R)
format theta_h mean_* sd_* p5 p95 bias mcse %9.6f
list rho h theta_h mean_ctrl bias mcse sd_ctrl p5 p95 ///
    mean_noctrl sd_noctrl, clean noobs
save output/mc_R${R}_summary, replace

* checks
assert sd_noctrl > sd_ctrl if rho == 0.9   // the control buys precision
assert abs(bias) < 3*mcse if rho == 0.5 & h <= 4
if $R == 200 {
    assert abs(mean_ctrl - 0.370337) < 1e-6 if rho == 0.9 & h == 8
    assert abs(sd_ctrl   - 0.211226) < 1e-6 if rho == 0.9 & h == 8
}
display "Exercise 7: all assertions passed"
log close
```

Two runs took 27.3 and 27.8 seconds in StataNow/SE 19.5, and every assertion
passed in both. The
no-control regressions use $200-h$ rows, one more than the controlled ones,
because they do not need $y_0$; this matches the design behind the notes' table.
Selected rows of the summary, rounded to four decimals:

| $\rho$ | $h$ | $\theta_h$ | Mean | MCSE | SD | 5th pct. | 95th pct. | Mean, no control | SD, no control |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0.5 | 0 | 1.0000 | 1.0028 | 0.0051 | 0.0717 | 0.8800 | 1.1171 | 0.9994 | 0.0970 |
| 0.5 | 4 | 0.0625 | 0.0507 | 0.0085 | 0.1208 | −0.1459 | 0.2439 | 0.0548 | 0.1217 |
| 0.5 | 8 | 0.0039 | −0.0169 | 0.0083 | 0.1173 | −0.2065 | 0.1901 | −0.0172 | 0.1178 |
| 0.5 | 12 | 0.0002 | −0.0105 | 0.0085 | 0.1197 | −0.2034 | 0.1764 | −0.0120 | 0.1206 |
| 0.9 | 0 | 1.0000 | 1.0031 | 0.0051 | 0.0720 | 0.8783 | 1.1135 | 0.9690 | 0.2209 |
| 0.9 | 4 | 0.6561 | 0.6279 | 0.0134 | 0.1899 | 0.3424 | 0.9418 | 0.6219 | 0.2651 |
| 0.9 | 8 | 0.4305 | 0.3703 | 0.0149 | 0.2112 | 0.0608 | 0.6944 | 0.3705 | 0.2568 |
| 0.9 | 12 | 0.2824 | 0.2303 | 0.0155 | 0.2185 | −0.1138 | 0.6167 | 0.2320 | 0.2449 |

**(a)** The log prints the asserted cell at full precision: at $\rho=0.9$ and
$h=8$ the mean is 0.370337 and the standard deviation 0.211226. Every
estimate is in units of $y$ per unit of $s$, and one unit of $s$ is one
standard deviation.

**(b)** The Monte Carlo standard error measures how far a simulated mean could
plausibly lie from the mean that unlimited replications would give. Divide
each gap between the mean estimate and $\theta_h$ by its MCSE, and read a ratio
beyond about two as more than simulation noise. At $\rho=0.9$ every mean from
$h=1$ to $h=12$ is below $\theta_h$, and the ratio passes two at $h=2$ and at
every horizon from $h=4$ on. The gap at $h=2$ is $-0.0233$, 2.2 standard errors;
at $h=4$ it is $-0.0282$, 2.1; from $h=5$ on, every gap is between 2.9 and 4.0
standard errors, the largest being $-0.0601$ at $h=8$. Only $h=0$, 1, and 3 stay
inside two. That is more than simulation noise: the estimator with $T=200$
falls systematically short at this persistence, by more at long horizons than
at short ones, which is the small-sample bias Lecture 2 takes up.

At $\rho=0.5$ the ratio also passes two at four horizons: $h=2$, 5, 7, and 8, at 2.2, 2.8,
2.0, and 2.5 standard errors, with the largest gap $-0.0241$ at $h=5$. These
gaps stay within 0.025 of $\theta_h$, about a fifth of the estimator's standard
deviation, and they do not grow with $h$. Thirteen correlated comparisons
easily produce a few ratios of that size, and the notes' $R=500$ run puts every
gap at $\rho=0.5$ within 0.014. A small shortfall at $\rho=0.5$ cannot be ruled
out, but at its largest it is less than half the one at $\rho=0.9$. One caution
applies to both readings: the thirteen means come from the same samples, so
their errors are correlated and the ratios are not thirteen independent
tests.

**(c)** With $\rho=0.9$ the control cuts the spread at impact by a factor of
three, from 0.2209 to 0.0720. Those are close to the large-sample values in the
notes, $\sqrt{9.53/200}=0.218$ and $1/\sqrt{199}=0.071$. The ratio of the two
standard deviations falls with the horizon, to 1.40 at $h=4$, 1.22 at $h=8$,
and 1.12 at $h=12$ (rounded to two decimals). The means with and without the
control are close at $h=4$, 8, and 12; the control changes the spread much
more than the centre.

The omitted term explains both patterns. Without the control, the residual
carries $\rho^{h+1}y_{t-1}$, whose variance is
$\rho^{2(h+1)}\operatorname{Var}(y)$ with
$\operatorname{Var}(y)=(\theta_0^2\sigma_s^2+\sigma_v^2)/(1-\rho^2)$. At
$\rho=0.9$, $\operatorname{Var}(y)=10.53$, and the added variance is still 3.67
at $h=4$. At $\rho=0.5$, $\operatorname{Var}(y)=2.67$ and the added variance at
$h=4$ is 0.0026. So at $\rho=0.5$ the control matters most at impact, 0.0717
against 0.0970, a little at $h=1$ and $h=2$, where the ratios are 1.13 and 1.07,
and hardly at all after that.
From $h=4$ on the two standard deviations are within one percent of each other,
and at $h=5$ and $h=6$ the one without the control is even slightly smaller,
which is simulation noise.

**(d)** In Exercise 6, $\hat\beta_8=0.240595$ lies inside the band from 0.0608
to 0.6944, below the centre but not unusually so. At $h=12$,
$\hat\beta_{12}=-0.293297$ lies below the 5th percentile, $-0.1138$. The same
sample is ordinary at one horizon and unusual four horizons later. That fits
what the notes say about the residual: neighbouring estimates share rows and
residual terms, so a sample that starts low tends to stay low and can drift
out of the band.

<!-- D32: the seed-2 sample was fixed before any estimate was seen and is kept
     although it leaves the band at h = 11 and h = 12. -->

*Seeding inside the loop.* Putting `set seed 3` inside the replication loop resets
the generator in every replication. Each replication then draws the same
sample, so the experiment is a single seed-3 sample estimated two hundred
times. A standard deviation of exactly zero at every horizon is the symptom.
:::
::::

### Exercise 8: What the residual contains {.unnumbered .exercise-title #exercise-l01-8}

::: {.exercise}
**Problem.** [core, pencil] In the AR(1) economy with $\theta_0=\sigma_s=\sigma_v=1$,
the horizon-$h$ residual of the regression on $(1,s_t,y_{t-1})$ is
$u_{t,h}=\sum_{j=0}^{h}\rho^{h-j}v_{t+j}+\sum_{j=1}^{h}\rho^{h-j}s_{t+j}$.

(a) Write $u_{t,1}$ and $u_{t+1,1}$ term by term, list the terms they share, and
derive $\operatorname{Corr}(u_{t,1},u_{t+1,1})$ as a function of $\rho$.

(b) Write $u_{t,2}$ and $u_{t+k,2}$ for $k=1,2,3$. Count the shared terms and
compute $\operatorname{Corr}(u_{t,2},u_{t+k,2})$ at $\rho=0.5$ for each $k$.

(c) Explain in one or two sentences why the correlation is zero beyond lag $h$.

(d) Show that $\mathbb E[s_tu_{t,2}\,s_{t+1}u_{t+1,2}]=0$, even though
$u_{t,2}$ and $u_{t+1,2}$ are correlated.
:::

:::: {.solution-material}
::: {.callout-tip .exercise-hint collapse="true" icon=false}
## Hint

Write the two residuals one above the other, aligned by date, with each term's
weight. A covariance collects only the terms that appear in both rows, and each
shared term contributes the product of its two weights.
:::

::: {.callout-note .exercise-solution collapse="true" icon=false}
## Detailed solution

Every term of a residual is either a disturbance $v$ or an intervention $s$,
each with variance one, and all of them are mutually independent (A2 and A3).
So the variance of a residual is the sum of its squared weights, and the
covariance of two residuals is the sum, over the terms they share, of the
products of the two weights. Nothing else enters.

**(a)** At $h=1$,

$$
u_{t,1}=\rho\,v_t+v_{t+1}+s_{t+1},
\qquad
u_{t+1,1}=\rho\,v_{t+1}+v_{t+2}+s_{t+2}.
$$

The rows share one term, $v_{t+1}$, with weight 1 in row $t$ and weight $\rho$ in
row $t+1$. Each variance is $\rho^2+1+1=2+\rho^2$, and the covariance is
$1\times\rho=\rho$. Hence

$$
\operatorname{Corr}(u_{t,1},u_{t+1,1})=\frac{\rho}{2+\rho^2},
$$

which at $\rho=0.5$ is $0.5/2.25=2/9=0.2222$ (rounded to four decimals).

**(b)** At $h=2$ the terms and weights are:

| Residual | $v_t$ | $v_{t+1}$ | $v_{t+2}$ | $v_{t+3}$ | $v_{t+4}$ | $s_{t+1}$ | $s_{t+2}$ | $s_{t+3}$ | $s_{t+4}$ |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| $u_{t,2}$ | $\rho^2$ | $\rho$ | 1 | | | $\rho$ | 1 | | |
| $u_{t+1,2}$ | | $\rho^2$ | $\rho$ | 1 | | | $\rho$ | 1 | |
| $u_{t+2,2}$ | | | $\rho^2$ | $\rho$ | 1 | | | $\rho$ | 1 |

and $u_{t+3,2}$ contains $v_{t+3},v_{t+4},v_{t+5}$ and $s_{t+4},s_{t+5}$. The
variance of each residual is

$$
\operatorname{Var}(u_{t,2})=\rho^4+\rho^2+1+\rho^2+1=2+2\rho^2+\rho^4 .
$$

- *Lag 1.* Rows $t$ and $t+1$ share three terms: $v_{t+1}$ (weights $\rho$ and
  $\rho^2$), $v_{t+2}$ (1 and $\rho$), and $s_{t+2}$ (1 and $\rho$). The
  covariance is $\rho^3+\rho+\rho=2\rho+\rho^3$.
- *Lag 2.* Rows $t$ and $t+2$ share one term, $v_{t+2}$ (1 and $\rho^2$), so the
  covariance is $\rho^2$.
- *Lag 3.* Row $t+3$ begins at date $t+3$, after row $t$'s last term. Nothing
  is shared, and the covariance is zero.

At $\rho=0.5$ the variance is $2+0.5+0.0625=2.5625=41/16$, and

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Corr}(u_{t,2},u_{t+1,2})&=\frac{1.125}{2.5625}=\frac{18}{41}=0.4390,\\
\operatorname{Corr}(u_{t,2},u_{t+2,2})&=\frac{0.25}{2.5625}=\frac{4}{41}=0.0976,\\
\operatorname{Corr}(u_{t,2},u_{t+3,2})&=0,
\end{aligned}
$$

with the decimals rounded to four places. These are the $\rho=0.5$ entries of
the notes' table of residual autocorrelations, where the long simulated sample
gives 0.2213, 0.4375, 0.0980, and 0.0011. The same counting at $\rho=0.9$ gives
0.3203, 0.5914, and 0.1894, so the correlations grow with persistence.

**(c)** Row $t$'s residual contains terms dated $t$ through $t+h$, and row
$t+k$'s residual contains terms dated $t+k$ through $t+k+h$. For $k>h$ the two
windows do not overlap, and independent terms with no overlap have zero
covariance. The residual is therefore at most a moving average of order $h$.

**(d)** Look for $s_t$ in the product $s_t\,u_{t,2}\,s_{t+1}\,u_{t+1,2}$. It
appears once, as the first factor. It is not in $u_{t,2}$, whose interventions
start at $s_{t+1}$; it is not $s_{t+1}$; and it is not in $u_{t+1,2}$. By A2 and
A3, $s_t$ is independent of the other three factors, so

$$
\mathbb E\bigl[s_tu_{t,2}\,s_{t+1}u_{t+1,2}\bigr]
=\mathbb E[s_t]\;\mathbb E\bigl[u_{t,2}\,s_{t+1}u_{t+1,2}\bigr]=0 .
$$

Because each product also has mean zero, the covariance of the two products is
zero while the residuals themselves have correlation 0.4390. The estimation
error of $\hat\beta_h$ is a weighted sum of residuals with weights built from
the interventions, so it is these products, not the bare residuals, whose
dependence matters for its variance. Lecture 5 builds standard errors on that
fact.

A frequent error is to leave the interventions $s_{t+1},\dots,s_{t+h}$ out
of the residual. At $h=2$ and lag 1 that drops one shared term and two variance
terms, and gives $(\rho^3+\rho)/(\rho^4+\rho^2+1)=0.625/1.3125=0.4762$ at
$\rho=0.5$ instead of 0.4390. Another is to conclude from correlated residuals
that $\hat\beta_h$ is biased; part (d) and the orthogonality conditions of
[Exercise 2](#exercise-l01-2) show why it is not.
:::
::::

### Exercise 9: First contact with military news {.unnumbered .exercise-title #exercise-l01-9}

::: {.exercise}
**Problem.** [data, computational] Ramey and Zubairy's quarterly U.S. data are
in the workbook `RZDAT.xlsx`, sheet `rzdat`, from their February 2018 replication
package. The course does not redistribute the file; the Practicum 01 lab project
ships `data/raw/get_rz.do`, which downloads it from the authors' archive,
checks its SHA-256, and prints manual download steps if the download fails. The
variables you need are `quarter` (fractional years), `rgdp` (real GDP) and
`rgdp_pott6` (trend GDP, the series the authors call potential GDP and estimate
as a sixth-degree polynomial trend in real GDP), both in billions of chained
2009 dollars at an annual rate, `pgdp` (the GDP deflator), and `news` (military
news, billions of nominal dollars).

(a) Run `get_rz.do`, import the sheet, keep quarters from 1889Q1 on, and declare
quarterly dates.

(b) Construct $y_t=\texttt{rgdp}_t/\texttt{rgdp\_pott6}_t$ and
$s_t=\texttt{news}_t/(\texttt{rgdp\_pott6}_{t-1}\times\texttt{pgdp}_{t-1})$.
Assert that $s_t$ has 504 nonmissing values.

(c) Estimate the local projection of $y_{t+h}$ on a constant, $s_t$, and
$y_{t-1}$ for $h=0,\dots,20$, storing $\hat\beta_h$ and $T_h$. Assert
$T_h=504-h$ and explain why the formula $T_h=T-h-p$, applied with $T=504$
quarters of news and $p=1$, seems to predict one row fewer. Report
$\hat\beta_8$, $\hat\beta_{10}$, and the peak horizon.

(d) On the $h=8$ estimation sample, compute each quarter's share of
$\sum_t(s_t-\bar s)^2$ and list the six largest.

(e) Re-estimate the $h=8$ regression without 1950Q3. Does removing Korea's news
quarter raise or lower the estimate?

(f) Draw the response graph and write its caption. Then write a paragraph of
five sentences headed "What has not yet been argued": one sentence each on
units, controls, identification, uncertainty, and dependence on a few episodes.
:::

:::: {.solution-material}
::: {.callout-tip .exercise-hint collapse="true" icon=false}
## Hint

Date the news by the quarter in which it arrived, and the control one quarter
earlier. Before running any loop, list 1950Q2 and 1950Q3 and check by hand
that the 1950Q3 value of $s_t$ divides that quarter's news by 1950Q2's nominal
trend GDP.
:::

::: {.callout-note .exercise-solution collapse="true" icon=false}
## Detailed solution

<!-- D5 and D35: RZDAT.xlsx is fetched by get_rz.do and never shipped. D33: the
     solution quotes estimates and six news values, not data rows. D40: the
     units of the news variable follow the notes, which checked them against
     Ramey (2011) and Ramey and Zubairy's documentation. -->

The do-file repeats the notes' first contact with data, starting from the raw
workbook. It adds a check wherever a quarterly data set can go wrong: the date
sequence, the timing of the scaling, the row count, and one coefficient that an
independent source can confirm.

```stata
* ex09_first_contact.do  Lecture 01, Exercise 9: first contact with data
* Run from the lab project's top folder with StataNow/SE 19.5.
version 19
clear all
set more off
capture log close
log using output/ex09_first_contact.txt, text replace

* 1. Data: fetch the workbook or verify the copy already there (D5, D35)
do data/raw/get_rz.do "data/raw"
import excel using data/raw/RZDAT.xlsx, sheet("rzdat") firstrow clear
drop if quarter < 1889
generate qdate = yq(1889, 1) + _n - 1
format qdate %tq
tsset qdate, quarterly
assert _N == 508
assert abs(quarter - (1889 + (_n - 1)/4)) < 1e-6   // consecutive quarters

* 2. Outcome, intervention, and (for the check in step 6) spending:
*    y = real GDP / trend GDP, newsy = news / lagged nominal trend GDP,
*    g = real government spending / trend GDP
generate double y     = rgdp/rgdp_pott6
generate double newsy = news/(L.rgdp_pott6*L.pgdp)
generate double g     = (ngov/pgdp)/rgdp_pott6
quietly count if newsy < .
assert r(N) == 504
quietly count if newsy != 0 & newsy < .
display "quarters with nonzero news: " r(N)
summarize y newsy

* 3. One regression per horizon, h = 0,...,20
tempname P
postfile `P' h double beta_h T_h using output/first_contact, replace
forvalues h = 0/20 {
    quietly regress F`h'.y newsy L.y
    post `P' (`h') (_b[newsy]) (e(N))
}
postclose `P'

* 4. Where the variation comes from: shares in the h = 8 sample
quietly regress F8.y newsy L.y
generate byte in8 = e(sample)
quietly summarize newsy if in8
generate double dev2 = (newsy - r(mean))^2 if in8
quietly summarize dev2
generate double share = dev2/r(sum)
gsort -share
generate double cumshare = sum(share)
format newsy share cumshare %9.6f
list qdate newsy share cumshare in 1/6, clean noobs
assert qdate[1] == tq(1941q4) & abs(share[1] - 0.261211) < 1e-6
assert qdate[2] == tq(1950q3) & abs(share[2] - 0.195838) < 1e-6
sort qdate

* 5. Drop one episode at h = 8
quietly regress F8.y newsy L.y if qdate != tq(1950q3)
display "h = 8 without 1950Q3: " %9.6f _b[newsy] "  (T_8 = " e(N) ")"
assert e(N) == 495 & abs(_b[newsy] - 0.433969) < 1e-6

* 6. Check against a source record: Ramey and Zubairy's controls at h = 10
*    equal irf_gdp_linear in the REP04 benchmark (their jordagk.do)
quietly regress F10.y newsy L(1/4).newsy L(1/4).y L(1/4).g
display "h = 10 with RZ controls: " %10.8f _b[newsy] "  (N = " e(N) ")"
assert e(N) == 490 & abs(_b[newsy] - 0.29376385) < 1e-6

* 7. The response, its checks, and the graph
use output/first_contact, clear
assert T_h == 504 - h
assert abs(beta_h[9]  - 0.361906) < 1e-6        // h = 8
assert abs(beta_h[11] - 0.404210) < 1e-6        // h = 10
quietly summarize beta_h
assert beta_h[11] == r(max)                     // the peak is at h = 10
format beta_h %9.6f
list h T_h beta_h, clean noobs

twoway connected beta_h h, lcolor(navy) mcolor(navy) msize(small)      ///
       yline(0, lcolor(gs13)) xlabel(0(4)20)                          ///
       ylabel(0(0.1)0.5, format(%3.1f) angle(0))                      ///
       xtitle("Quarters after the news arrives")                      ///
       ytitle("Percent of trend GDP, per news worth 1 percent")       ///
       graphregion(color(white)) plotregion(color(white))
graph export output/ex09_first_contact.pdf, replace
display "Exercise 9: all assertions passed"
log close
```

In the verification run the workbook was already in `data/raw`, and
`get_rz.do` reported "Ramey-Zubairy data present in data/raw and verified
(SHA-256)." Every later assertion passed.

**(a)–(b)** The sheet holds 564 rows; dropping those before 1889 leaves 508
consecutive quarters, 1889Q1–2015Q4, and the date assertion confirms that no
quarter is missing or repeated. The log's summary gives $y_t$ a mean of 0.9868665
over 508 quarters and $s_t$ a mean of 0.0072219 and standard deviation
0.0597282 over 504 quarters, 108 of them nonzero. The four missing values of
$s_t$ are the 1889 quarters, where `news` is missing. A unit of $s_t$ is news
worth a full year of nominal trend GDP, so the natural reading unit is 0.01,
news worth one percent of trend GDP.

**(c)** The assertion $T_h=504-h$ passes. The formula $T_h=T-h-p$ with $T=504$
and $p=1$ would give $503-h$, but it counts a lag as a lost row only when the
lagged variable begins where the sample does. Here the first row with news is
1890Q1, and $y_{t-1}$ exists there because GDP starts four quarters earlier.
The lag costs nothing, and each horizon still costs one row at the end. The
estimates rise from $\hat\beta_0=0.080313$ to $\hat\beta_4=0.259141$ and
$\hat\beta_8=0.361906$, peak at $\hat\beta_{10}=0.404210$, and fall to
$\hat\beta_{20}=0.079552$. News worth one percent of trend GDP moves $s_t$ by
0.01 and the prediction for $y_{t+h}$ by $0.01\hat\beta_h$; since $y$ is a ratio
to trend GDP, that is $\hat\beta_h$ percent of trend GDP. Ten quarters after such
news, GDP is about 0.40 percent of trend GDP above what the regression
otherwise predicts from the previous quarter's output.

**(d)** The six largest shares of $\sum_t(s_t-\bar s)^2$ in the $h=8$ sample
(496 quarters, 1890Q1–2013Q4) are, as the log lists them:

```text
     qdate      newsy      share   cumshare
    1941q4   0.691893   0.261211   0.261211
    1950q3   0.600073   0.195838   0.457049
    1942q3   0.432791   0.100897   0.557946
    1950q4   0.402163   0.086893   0.644839
    1917q2   0.372915   0.074496   0.719335
    1941q2   0.340130   0.061734   0.781069
```

Two quarters supply 45.7 percent of the variation and six supply 78.1 percent.
The shares use $s_t-\bar s$, as in the notes' slope formula; with $y_{t-1}$ in
the regression the exact weights use $s_t$ purged of $y_{t-1}$, which is close
but not identical.

**(e)** Without 1950Q3 the $h=8$ estimate is 0.433969 on 495 rows, against
0.361906 on the full sample. Removing Korea's news quarter *raises* the
estimate by 0.072. Measured against the regression's average relation, what
followed the Korean news eight quarters later was smaller than what followed
the other large episodes, so that quarter was pulling the slope down.

*Check against a source record.* With Ramey and Zubairy's own controls (four lags
each of the news, $y$, and government spending relative to trend), the $h=10$
coefficient is 0.29376385 on 490 rows. That equals, at $10^{-6}$, the linear GDP response
`irf_gdp_linear` at $h=10$ in the course's REP04 benchmark. The benchmark comes
from an unmodified run of the authors' `jordagk.do`, lines 253–386 and 398–417
of the frozen package. The data construction therefore matches the
authors' to the digits shown, and the difference from 0.404 comes from the
controls, not from the data.

**(f)** The exported graph is a hump: 0.08 at impact, a peak of 0.40 at ten
quarters, and 0.08 again at twenty. A caption that states what the reader needs:

> Response of real GDP, in percent of trend GDP, to military-spending news worth
> one percent of the previous quarter's nominal trend GDP. Local projections of
> $y_{t+h}$ on a constant, the news, and $y_{t-1}$, 1890Q1–2015Q4, with
> $T_h=504-h$ rows at horizon $h$. Horizons are quarters after the news
> arrives. Read causally, the vertical axis is the gap between GDP and the path
> it would have followed without the news, a reading not yet argued. No bands
> are shown.

A paragraph that lists, without defending, what the graph has not earned:

> *What has not yet been argued.* The coefficients are responses of a level
> relative to a fitted trend per unit of scaled news, and whether that level,
> its change, or its accumulation answers the policymaker's question is not yet
> settled. One lag of GDP is a choice, and Ramey and Zubairy's controls lower
> the ten-quarter coefficient from 0.404 to 0.294. Reading the curve as the
> effect of the news requires the news to be unpredictable and unrelated to the
> taxes, monetary policy, price controls, and wars that arrived with it, which
> nothing here has shown. No standard error or band has been computed, and the
> overlapping horizons make the residuals serially correlated. Two quarters,
> 1941Q4 and 1950Q3, supply 45.7 percent of the variation in the news, and
> dropping 1950Q3 alone moves the eight-quarter estimate from 0.362 to 0.434.

Each sentence points to a later lecture: units to Lecture 2, controls and
identification to Lectures 3 and 4, uncertainty to Lectures 5 and 6, and
episode dependence to Lecture 13.

Two mistakes are predictable. The first is a timing slip in the scaling:
dividing the news by the *same* quarter's nominal trend GDP, or lagging the
news itself instead of its denominator. Either changes the variable the notes
define, the second also dates every episode a quarter late, and the hand check
on 1950Q3 in the hint catches both. The second mistake is to assert
$T_h=503-h$ from the formula and then "fix" the data until it passes, which
throws away a quarter of real data. The formula
counts rows that are missing; it does not decide which rows should be.
:::
::::

### Exercise 10: Korea is not the average {.unnumbered .exercise-title #exercise-l01-10}

::: {.exercise}
**Problem.** [extra, pencil] In the Ramey–Zubairy data, GDP relative to trend
was $y=0.972500$ in 1950Q2, and the news in 1950Q3 was $s=0.600073$ of lagged
nominal trend GDP. Later values of $y$ were 1.000572 in 1950Q3, 1.033931 in
1951Q3, and 1.051212 in 1953Q1. The first-contact local projection of
[Exercise 9](#exercise-l01-9) gives $\hat\beta_0=0.080313$,
$\hat\beta_4=0.259141$, and $\hat\beta_{10}=0.404210$.

(a) For $h=0,4,10$, compute the realized change $y_{1950Q3+h}-y_{1950Q2}$ and
the scaled coefficient $0.600073\,\hat\beta_h$, both in units of trend GDP.

(b) Which of the two numbers, if either, measures a gap between two paths?

(c) Give three distinct reasons why the two numbers differ, and say what
follows if both are taken at face value.
:::

:::: {.solution-material}
::: {.callout-tip .exercise-hint collapse="true" icon=false}
## Hint

Write each number as a difference between two outcomes, and label each outcome
with its date and with the path it lies on, realized or counterfactual. For
(c), look for reasons on both sides: in what the realized change contains, and
in what the coefficient averages and assumes.
:::

::: {.callout-note .exercise-solution collapse="true" icon=false}
## Detailed solution

**(a)** Subtracting and multiplying,

| $h$ | Quarter | $y$ | Realized change | $\hat\beta_h$ | $0.600073\,\hat\beta_h$ | Ratio |
|---:|:---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 1950Q3 | 1.000572 | 0.0281 | 0.080313 | 0.0482 | 1.72 |
| 4 | 1951Q3 | 1.033931 | 0.0614 | 0.259141 | 0.1555 | 2.53 |
| 10 | 1953Q1 | 1.051212 | 0.0787 | 0.404210 | 0.2426 | 3.08 |

The changes and products are rounded to four decimals, which gives the same
digits whether they are computed from the six-decimal inputs or from the
unrounded data. From the unrounded data, the realized changes are 0.028072,
0.061430, and 0.078712, and the scaled coefficients 0.048194, 0.155503, and
0.242556 (six decimals); the ratio column uses those values. Both columns are in
units of trend GDP, so the last realized change is the 7.87 points of the notes'
opening, and the scaled coefficient is about three times larger.

**(b)** The realized change is not a gap between paths. It compares one path
with itself at two dates, and by the decomposition in the notes' first section
it equals the causal response plus the change GDP would have made without the
news:

$$
y_{t+h}-y_{t-1}=\theta_h\,s_t+\bigl(y^{c}_{t+h}-y_{t-1}\bigr).
$$

The scaled coefficient estimates $0.600073\,\beta_h$, and that equals a gap,
$\theta_h\,s_t$, only under conditions this lecture has not established for the
news. The news would have to
be an observed shock, its effects would have to be linear and the same in every
episode, and one lag of GDP would have to be an adequate control.

**(c)** Three distinct reasons:

1. *Everything else in 1950–1953.* The realized change contains the
   counterfactual change: tax increases, the Treasury–Federal Reserve Accord,
   wage and price controls, and the war itself apart from its spending news.
   A path comparison removes those; a change along one path keeps them.
2. *An average applied to one episode.* $\hat\beta_{10}$ averages over every
   quarter with news, weighted by $(s_t-\bar s)^2$; in the eight-quarter
   sample of Exercise 9, 1941Q4 alone carries 26 percent of that weight.
   Exercise 9 also found that dropping 1950Q3 raises the eight-quarter
   estimate, so eight quarters after its news Korea's own outcome sat below the
   average relation. Multiplying the average by Korea's news also assumes that news
   worth 60 percent of trend GDP has sixty times the effect of news worth one
   percent, whatever the state of the economy (A1).
3. *Specification and identification.* The coefficient depends on the controls:
   with Ramey and Zubairy's, $0.600073\times0.29376385=0.1763$ (rounded), already
   a quarter lower. And the reading of any coefficient as $\theta_h$ rests on an
   identification argument that Lecture 3 has yet to make. Neither number
   carries a measure of uncertainty.

Taken at face value together, the decomposition says that without the news GDP
relative to trend would have *fallen* by $0.242556-0.078712=0.163844$ between
1950Q2 and 1953Q1, about sixteen points of trend GDP (unrounded values). Nobody has argued that, and the
tension is a reason to doubt at least one of the maintained assumptions rather
than to pick the more convenient number.

Watch for a units slip: scaling by 60.0073 because the news is
"60 percent" of trend GDP. That gives 24.26 at $h=10$, a number one hundred times
too large, because $s_t$ is measured as a fraction, not in percent. A second slip
is to conclude that the regression overstates the effect threefold. Neither column
is the effect of Korea's news.
